content: The annex provides interim guidelines for treating tuberculosis (TB) in young children weighing less than 25 kg. These guidelines utilize currently available fixed-dose combinations of anti-TB drugs (Rifampicin/Isoniazid/Pyrazinamide in a 60/30/150 mg formulation) and recommend dosages based on weight bands. The second edition of the Guidance for National Tuberculosis Programmes on the Management of Tuberculosis in Children outlines its purpose and target audience. It highlights the differences between TB in children and adolescents compared to adults and provides an estimate of the burden of childhood TB. The guidance is intended to assist national TB control programs, pediatricians, and healthcare workers in managing TB in children and in families affected by TB. The first edition of this guidance, published in 2006, was instrumental in supporting lowand middle-income countries in developing or revising their national guidelines for managing childhood TB. Since 2006, the World Health Organization (WHO) has issued numerous recommendations relevant to managing TB and TB/HIV in children, as well as children living in TB-affected families. The second edition consolidates all relevant recommendations into a single document. The updated guidance aims to improve case detection, treatment outcomes, and the recording and reporting of childhood TB cases by national TB programs. It is specifically targeted at lowand middle-income countries with a medium to high TB burden and is not intended for high-income countries with low TB prevalence. This distinction is particularly important for diagnostic approaches and contact investigations. The guidance is designed to inform the development or revision of national guidelines to ensure early identification and effective management of TB infection and disease in children based on the best available evidence. It also aims to facilitate the implementation and scaling-up of current policies and activities, such as contact investigation and isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT), while bridging the gap between policy and practice. Children with TB often present with pulmonary TB, the most common form, but extrapulmonary TB is also frequent, accounting for 30-40% of cases. Infants and young children, particularly those under two years of age, are at the highest risk of developing severe, disseminated TB disease, which is associated with high morbidity and mortality. Adolescents, on the other hand, are more likely to develop adult-type pulmonary TB, which is often sputum smear-positive and infectious, making them a source of transmission. The presentation of TB in children is an indicator of recent and ongoing transmission of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the community. Infants may present with acute symptoms resembling severe or persistent pneumonia, and TB should be suspected when there is a poor response to conventional antibiotics. Adolescents with TB often face unique psychosocial challenges, including issues with autonomy, adherence to treatment, and transitioning from pediatric to adult healthcare services. Ethical considerations are critical in implementing TB control strategies or conducting research involving children. Governments are obligated to provide universal access to high-quality TB diagnosis and treatment and address the social determinants responsible for TB transmission. Communities play a vital role in supporting TB diagnosis and treatment, ensuring equitable access to healthcare, and fostering a stigma-free environment. The burden of childhood TB remains largely unknown, although WHO estimated in 2012 that there were 530,000 TB cases among children under 15 years of age globally, with 74,000 deaths among HIV-negative children. These figures represent 6% and 8% of the global totals, respectively. The second edition of the guidance was developed following WHO's evidence-based guideline development procedures, including the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. This process involved a systematic review of literature, consultation with experts, and evaluation of recent evidence to update recommendations. The guidance incorporates new topics such as the use of novel diagnostics like Xpert MTB/RIF, interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs), revised drug dosages for children, BCG vaccination in HIV-endemic settings, and the management of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) in children. The recommendations were reviewed and graded based on the quality of evidence, patient values, preferences, and cost considerations. The final recommendations were either accepted unchanged or revised, with the aim of improving TB prevention, care, and control activities for children in resource-limited settings.
